doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

title: Learning harmony from Walter Bishop Jr. and Don Pullen
summary: Bishop's harmonic influence and book, Pullen's melodic and avant-garde inside-the-blues approach; she absorbed from the masters.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Working with all those established piano players must have increased your already developed hearing because Don Pullen is not going to play all the same changes that Walter Bishop Junior is even though the tune may be the same. Did you find that you followed them when they went to different places or did you try to like just stick to what you knew?

This is, you know jazz is such a wonderful experiment where we’re exploring possibilities all the time. It’s the nature of the music you know. And I’m young and I’m anxious and I’m learning and I want to be liked, I want to be known and recognized for being a musician not just a singer myself you see and that little arranging part, there’s something so wonderful and diplomatic and democratic about the experience of this music and to stay open to the possibilities. And you think you might be on this certain track with the Walter Bishop — and Walter by the way, I took piano lessons with him for a while. And if not for Walter Bishop Junior I think a lot of the things that happened in my harmonic construction would not be there in my music. Now Don Pullen on the other hand, I never, I mean I think my first gig with Don might have been at Jazzmania. But when I got that gig in Harlem a few years later there was no piano anywhere to be — it was all organ. So that’s a whole different vibe in itself and Don was always on the edge but he was what I call — anybody who’s known for their avant garde or playing on the outside, that’s the reason that is — Albert Ayler is another example of that, it’s because they are so, they come from inside. They come from, you know, the depths of the blues, the intricate, you know, spiritual aspects of Gospel music. So when they go out on the edge and they’re experimenting like that, or expressing themselves that way, it’s not some random sort of like oh pick a note any note. It’s not like that at all. It’s really from a centered place, this expression is an evolution of that, that simplistic approach that we start with at the piano. C-E-G triads or what have you. And then you discover the flat seventh oh my God, the flatted seventh is everything, you know the tritone. My God, the tritone. That interval in and of itself you know. And actually Walter Bishop Junior did publish a book, A Study in Fourths it’s called, by Walter Bishop Junior. And the entire book is nothing but all of these things he derived from just playing perfect fourths. And you know there are famous tunes that I can recall like “Witch Hunt” [scats] you know, that phase, that time where bebop and modern jazz were kind of at this wonderful precipice and sort of like playing off each other. There are a lot of things that I got from Walter Bishop Junior that are very much a part of how I approach harmony to this day. And then there’s Don whose melodic sensibilities are ridiculous. And they had their own trios and if you heard, if you ever heard Don Pullen, with Adams and Danny Richmond — you know what can I say. So my, you know we’re talking, now check this out, everything we’re talking about has nothing to do with the singers. I’m not even talking

about singers yet, okay? We haven’t even talked about the Ellas and the Sarahs and the Carmen McRaes and the Bettys and all that. Okay? This is just how the music — I think I was a sponge, I think I still am. I was just absorbing from the masterful, from the masters really, of that time. I’m in my early twenties and they are fully realized artists at that time in their careers. And I’m just really taking whatever they offer and happy to be in the mix.
